title: Dedicated GPU pool - autoscale warmup debug scratchpad
content:
Context / summary:
- Scratchpad for debugging recurring capacity-thrash incidents in the dedicated GPU pool during warmup. Mostly notes-to-self + commands/log snippets + hypotheses.
- Symptom: sudden p95/p99 token latency spikes and failed allocations when new capacity is added; autoscaler oscillates (scale-up -> scale-down quickly) causing models to be reloaded repeatedly. Customers see 5-20s spike and some 429s.

Timeline (recent incident 2026-02-22):
- 10:03 UTC: sustained incoming queue growth to ~300 requests/sec for a burst (ramping trial cluster).
- 10:05 UTC: autoscaler started adding nodes (pool-min=2, pool-max=10, target-util=0.65).
- 10:06-10:08 UTC: new nodes join but pods remain Pending -> node init logs show CUDA drivers loaded but nvidia-device-plugin CrashLoopBackOff on some nodes.
- 10:09 UTC: first model load on freshly scheduled pod (container started) -> model download + warmup starts (large model, ~6.1B). Model load takes ~40-120s.
- 10:10 UTC: scale-down triggered (controller thinks utilization dropped) and tries to evict underutilized nodes. Evictions hit pods still warming -> model load aborted, container restarted, cache lost.
- 10:11-10:14 UTC: repeat churn while traffic still above baseline.

Commands I ran (notes + results):
- kubectl top nodes --no-headers | sort -k3 -n -> confirms low GPU % on new nodes while CPU warmup tasks spike on init pods.
- kubectl get pods -n dedicated-pool -o wide | grep Pending -> revealed imagePullBackOff on nvidia-device-plugin occasionally.
- kubectl logs -n kube-system nvidia-device-plugin-xxx -> "failed to discover devices: timeout waiting for devices" followed by plugin restart. Some nodes had slow driver-binding at boot.
- curl -sS https://internal-metrics.redwood/api/pool/dedicatedgpu?since=10m | jq '.autoscaler_events[]' -> showed scale-down decisions at 10:09 with reason "utilization_below_target" despite queue length > threshold (bug?).
- oc adm cordon/uncordon not used here but I manually set pod disruption budget to 0.5 to test preventing eviction (see below).

Representative log snippets (redacted):
- kubelet: "device plugin registration failed: rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded"
- autoscaler: "RecommendScaleDown: pool utilization 0.32 < target 0.65 (10s window) -> scaleDown to 3"
- controller: "evicting pod dedicated/serve-abc-123 due to scaleDown"
- serve container: "[model-loader] download complete, starting load. estimated memory: 18.2GB"
- serve container: "OOMKill during warmup after SIGTERM"

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Cold model load time + autoscaler short window -> autoscaler misinterprets transient utilization drop and evicts before warmup completes. Node/pod warmup latency is longer for certain larger models (esp fp32).
2) Device plugin instability on certain instance images causes delayed GPU availability; autoscaler sees node as not ready and schedules replacement, further increasing churn.
3) Autoscaler logic currently uses aggregate GPU utilization over a short window; queue length + pending pods not included properly in decision. Scale decisions are too reactive.
4) Eviction termination sends SIGTERM and we don't have graceful warmup checkpointing; aborted warmup wastes time and increases re-load frequency -> amplifies churn.
5) Node boot time variance (spot vs on-demand mix) and imagePullBackOffs combine to produce partial capacity visibility during decision window.

Quick experiments attempted (results):
- Increase autoscaler window to 2m (test cluster): reduced churn but slower to react to real sustained drops. Observed fewer evictions during warmup.
- Set pool.min to 4 during burst: prevented scale-down but raised cost. Good as mitigation for predictable bursts.
- Add a warmup-probe: after model load finishes, pod flips readiness to true. Before that it's NotReady; autoscaler should ignore NotReady capacity. BUT our autoscaler counting logic included unready nodes in utilization calculation - possible bug.
- Adjust PDB (pod disruption budget) to require at most 1 eviction at a time for this pool: reduced simultaneous terminations, but evictions still aborted warmup when it did happen.
- Preload models on spare nodes during warmup window via maintenance job (cron): promising but needs disk/cache sizing and long-lived spare nodes.

Things to check / next steps:
- Verify autoscaler code path that computes "available_capacity": ensure it excludes nodes/pods with readiness=false. Link to suspected code: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/blob/main/src/scale_decider.py (PR in review).
- Investigate device-plugin crashloops on certain AMIs. Ask infra to repro node boot sequence and confirm GPU drivers + plugin versions. Possible image roll required.
- Add instrumentation: emit event when model_load_started and model_load_finished with model_id, bytes_downloaded, duration. Then correlate with autoscaler events around same timestamps.
- Consider implementing a warmup grace window for scale-down decisions per-pool (e.g., if any pod has annotation "warmup_in_progress=true", autoscaler delays scale-down for X seconds). Simple and low-risk.
- Improve eviction behavior: instead of immediate SIGTERM, send SIGINT to serve process and wait longer for warmup checkpoint to persist, or mark pod as "do-not-evict" until warmup complete.
- Add queue-length as an input to autoscaler decision (current version oddly ignores pending queue if it sees low GPU utilization due to warmup).

Notes on customer impact and mitigation:
- Short term: recommended to set pool.min to expected concurrency during experiments / known traffic bursts. Notify affected customers and disable aggressive auto-shrink for the pool.
- Medium term: patch autoscaler to ignore NotReady/uninitialized nodes and add warmup grace.
- Long term: pre-warm model caches (either persistent model cache on node or fast snapshot restore) and improve device-plugin reliability.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are we seeing this only on specific instance types (A100 vs H100)? Need GPU model mapping for incidents.
- How much of the load time is network (model download) vs actual CUDA init + weight deserialization? Add more fine-grained timers in loader.
- Can we survive with a two-tier model variant strategy: tiny-quantized for warmup + swap to larger model once warmed? Operational complexity high but possible.

Relevant tickets / logs:
- SERV-789 (incident) - timeline and customer reports
- PR #412 (serve-runtime): add model_load_finished event (in review)
- Slack thread C01234567 - internal debugging chat 2026-02-22

Action items (owner + ETA):
- Aisha: add model load instrumentation to runtime (PR opened) - ETA 2026-03-05
- Ben: reproduce device-plugin instability on AMI-2026-01-12 and note driver versions - ETA 2026-03-03
- Samir: propose autoscaler warmup-grace patch + tests (include not-ready exclusion) - ETA 2026-03-07
- Lila: run cost analysis for pool.min increased to 4 during bursts (customer-facing mitigation) - ETA 2026-03-04

Mental note: this doc is messy on purpose. Keep iterating here before making a cleaned-up postmortem in shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/.

Recent edits: 2026-03-02: added timeline details and device plugin logs.

-- end of scratchpad --
